scenes.heading: DEEPSEEK 4, ON *HARDWARE YOU OWN*
scenes.say: The creator of Redis built a small inference engine to run DeepSeek 4 on hardware people actually own.
The repo is {ds4|D S four}: twenty three thousand stars, MIT licensed, and its engine is called DwarfStar.

scenes.heading: WHAT IT *RUNS*
scenes.say: It runs DeepSeek 4 Flash and Pro, GLM five point two and five point three, even Qwen three point eight Flash Next.
Metal on Macs with ninety six gigs or more, CUDA on Nvidia cards including older Ada ones, and ROCm on Strix Halo. Smaller Macs can stream weights from an SSD.

scenes.heading: SERVING *MANY* USERS
scenes.label: aggregate · 8x L40S · 16 sessions · authors' setup
scenes.say: Their eight card L40S setup served sixteen sessions at about one hundred and twenty six tokens per second aggregate.

scenes.heading: THE *CATCH*
cons: Main Mac path wants 96 GB or more
scenes.say: The catches: it is not a general GGUF runner, you use its own quantized files; the main Mac path wants ninety six gigs or more; and support is deliberately narrow. It is MIT licensed, self-contained C, it runs models other backends cannot, and it says openly that it is built with AI assistance.
Would you run DeepSeek at home? Comment D S four and I will pin the repo.

DeepSeek 4 local inference, without a datacenter: antirez (the creator of Redis) ships ds4 / DwarfStar, an MIT-licensed C engine for DeepSeek 4 Flash and PRO, GLM 5.2-5.3 and Qwen3.8 Flash Next. Metal on Macs (96 GB+, SSD streaming below that), CUDA including Ada cards, ROCm on Strix Halo; the authors' eight-L40S setup hit ~126 t/s aggregate across 16 sessions. 23,783 stars as of 12 October 2026.
Source: https://github.com/antirez/ds4
